text: Name a dead or extinct language.
flavor: Words nobody speaks any more, carved into stone and clay. Some of them may still be listening.
rules: Any language with no native speakers left, ancient or recent. Revived languages count if they died out first, like Cornish.

answers.lore: Dead, though the Vatican still writes in it, and one of its cash machines offered instructions in Latin.
Cracked in 1822 by Champollion, using the Rosetta Stone.
Dolly Pentreath, who died in 1777, is often called its last native speaker. It has since been revived.
Its last native speaker, Ned Maddrell, died in 1974. It has since been revived.
One of the first languages ever written down, pressed into clay over 5,000 years ago.
We can read its letters, but understand only a few hundred of its words.
The language of Hammurabi's laws and of the Epic of Gilgamesh.
Forgotten for 3,000 years, until clay tablets in Turkey revealed the oldest written Indo-European language.
The last stage of Egyptian, still heard in the services of the Coptic Church.
Nobody's mother tongue for some 1,700 years, until Eliezer Ben-Yehuda raised his son in it in 1880s Jerusalem.
So little survives that scholars argued for a century over whether it was even Celtic.
Spoken in Orkney and Shetland until the 1700s or 1800s, a descendant of the Vikings' Norse.
Found in Buddhist texts in the deserts of western China, yet related to European languages.
Had around 80 consonants and only two or three vowels. Its last fluent speaker died in 1992.
Its last speaker, Tuone Udaina, was killed by a roadworks explosion in 1898.
A pidgin of mostly Italian and Spanish words, used by sailors, traders and captives around the Mediterranean for centuries.
Its last native speaker, Cristina Calderón, died in Chile in 2022.
Its last native speaker, Marie Smith Jones, died in Alaska in 2008.
A pidgin of Russian and Norwegian, used for some 150 years by Russian traders and Norwegian fishermen in the Arctic.
Deafness was so common on the island that hearing people signed too. Its last signers died in the mid-1900s.
Its last speaker, Boa Sr, died in 2010 on the Andaman Islands.
Still spoken in Crimea in the 1560s. All that survives is a list of about 80 words a Flemish diplomat wrote down.
A lost language of ancient Crete, written in Greek letters but still not understood.

traps.reason: Still alive: modern forms are spoken by hundreds of thousands of people.
Alive. Millions of people speak Mayan languages today.
Invented, and still very much alive.
Invented for fiction, and alive among fans.
Invented for horror stories. No one ever spoke it.
Alive, and spoken every day in the Gaeltacht.
Alive, with tens of thousands of speakers or more.
Alive, and older than any language around it.
Alive, and still close to the Norse of the sagas.
Alive. Its ancient form would have counted.
A script, not a language.
A code, not a language.
A people, not a language.
A people, not a language. Their language is still spoken.
A people, not a language. Their language is still spoken.
Alive, and spoken by millions in the Andes.
Alive, and spoken by well over a million people in Mexico.
A family of languages, some of them alive. Which one?
Alive, with hundreds of thousands of speakers.
Alive, and spoken by millions. Plain Hebrew counts: it died out as a mother tongue first.
Invented, and never anyone's mother tongue.
A word game played inside English, not a language of its own.
Alive, as Farsi, with tens of millions of speakers. Its older forms would have counted.
Alive, as the Slavic language of North Macedonia. Its ancient namesake would have counted.

source: Copied from the daily question "dead-languages" on 28 November 2026.
